title: Given a collection of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges.
topicTitle: Explain Bellman-Ford. How does it handle negative edge weights, how does it dete

s1_definition.profdef: Merging intervals takes a list of ranges, each with a start and end, and combines any that overlap into single continuous ranges, returning a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals. The standard approach sorts the intervals by start, then sweeps left to right, extending the current merged interval whenever the next one overlaps it and starting a fresh interval when it does not. Sorting dominates the cost at n log n, with a single linear pass to merge.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has many maintenance windows booked on a core system throughout a day, some of which overlap or touch, and it wants to know the actual blocks of time the system is unavailable. A planner first lines up all windows by start time. She holds the current block in mind, and for each next window she checks: does it start before the current block ends? If so, they overlap, so she stretches the current block's end to cover the later window. If the next window starts after the current block ends, there is a genuine gap, so she finalises the current block and starts a new one. The finalised blocks are the real outage periods.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, then sweep: extend the current interval when the next overlaps, otherwise close it and begin a new one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merging intervals takes a list of ranges, each with a start and end, and combines any that overlap into single continuous ranges, returning a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals. The standard approach sorts the intervals by start, then sweeps left to right, extending the current merged interval whenever the next one overlaps it and starting a fresh interval when it does not. Sorting dominates the cost at n log n, with a single linear pass to merge.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has many maintenance windows booked on a core system throughout a day, some of which overlap or touch, and it wants to know the actual blocks of time the system is unavailable. A planner first lines up all windows by start time. She holds the current block in mind, and for each next window she checks: does it start before the current block ends? If so, they overlap, so she stretches the current block's end to cover the later window. If the next window starts after the current block ends, there is a genuine gap, so she finalises the current block and starts a new one. The finalised blocks are the real outage periods.

**One line to remember:** Sort by start, then sweep: extend the current interval when the next overlaps, otherwise close it and begin a new one.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason sorting is the first step is that it makes overlap detection local. Once intervals are ordered by start time, you only ever need to compare the next interval against the single current merged interval, never against all previous ones, because any interval that could overlap the next one has already been folded into the current one.

After sorting by start, you initialise the current merged interval to the first interval. Then you iterate the rest. For each interval, you compare its start to the current interval's end. If the start is less than or equal to the current end, they overlap or touch, so you merge by extending the current end to the maximum of the two ends: `currentEnd = Math.max(currentEnd, next.end);`. Taking the maximum is important because the next interval might be entirely inside the current one, in which case the end should not shrink. If the start is greater than the current end, there is no overlap, so you push the current interval to the result and make the next interval the new current.

The choice of less-than-or-equal versus strictly-less-than for the overlap test depends on whether touching intervals, where one ends exactly when the next begins, should be merged; for contiguous time blocks they usually should, so less-than-or-equal is typical. After the loop you must remember to push the final current interval, which is the common off-by-one bug if forgotten. The total cost is n log n for the sort plus a linear merge pass, and the output is at most as large as the input.

A senior-level nuance is where this pattern recurs: it is the backbone of interval scheduling, calendar and booking systems, memory-range coalescing, and genomic range merging. Related problems reuse the sorted-sweep idea, such as inserting a new interval into a sorted non-overlapping set, finding free gaps, or counting maximum concurrent intervals, which leads into the meeting-rooms problem. For money or precise timestamps I compare with the appropriate type, using compareTo for BigDecimal or Instant comparisons for times.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India schedules maintenance windows on a core banking system, and overlapping or contiguous windows must be coalesced into the true continuous outage periods so customer communications state accurate downtime. This is exactly merging overlapping intervals.

Problem 2 — A window fully contained inside another must not shorten the outage, and two windows that touch end-to-start should be reported as one continuous block. Taking the maximum end on merge handles containment, and the less-than-or-equal overlap test merges touching windows.

In our mini-project we build a `MaintenanceWindowMerger` over intervals represented as integer start-end pairs, standing for minutes from midnight. The demo merges several windows and logs the coalesced outage periods.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four windows in minutes, sixty to one twenty, one hundred to one fifty, two hundred to two forty, two forty to three hundred.

Step 1: Sort by start time. The windows are already in start order here: sixty to one twenty, one hundred to one fifty, two hundred to two forty, two forty to three hundred.

Step 2: Initialise the current interval to the first window, sixty to one twenty.

Step 3: Compare the second window, one hundred to one fifty. Its start one hundred is less than or equal to the current end one twenty, so they overlap. Extend the current end to the maximum of one twenty and one fifty, which is one fifty. The current interval is now sixty to one fifty.

Step 4: Compare the third window, two hundred to two forty. Its start two hundred is greater than the current end one fifty, so there is a gap. Push the current interval sixty to one fifty to the result and make the current interval two hundred to two forty.

Step 5: Compare the fourth window, two forty to three hundred. Its start two forty is less than or equal to the current end two forty, so they touch. Extend the current end to the maximum of two forty and three hundred, which is three hundred. The current interval is now two hundred to three hundred.

Step 6: The loop ends, so push the final current interval two hundred to three hundred. The result is two coalesced outages, sixty to one fifty and two hundred to three hundred, correctly merging the overlap and the touching windows.

```
[2026-10-26 23:38:01] INFO    Coalesced outages: [[60, 150], [200, 300]]
```

```
      Pre:  each interval [start ≤ end]

  ── State Diagram: Sweep ─────────────────────────────────

  [next.start ≤ current.end] ──→ extend current.end = max(...)
  [next.start > current.end]  ──→ push current; current = next
  [end of list] ──→ push final current

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. merge: sort by start
  2.   current = first
  3.   for each next: overlap→extend; gap→push+reset
  4.   push final current; return
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging intervals takes a list of ranges, each with a start and end, and combines any overlapping ones into single continuous ranges, returning a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals. The first and most important step is to sort the intervals by start time, because sorting makes overlap detection local: once the intervals are ordered, I only ever need to compare the next interval against the single current merged interval, never against all the earlier ones.

After sorting, I set the current interval to the first one and sweep through the rest. For each interval I compare its start to the current interval's end. If the start is at or before the current end, they overlap or touch, so I merge by extending the current end to the maximum of the two ends, and taking the maximum matters because the next interval might sit entirely inside the current one, in which case the end must not shrink. If the start is beyond the current end, there is a real gap, so I push the current interval to the result and start a new current. After the loop I must remember to push the final current interval, which is the classic off-by-one bug if forgotten. The cost is n log n for the sort plus a linear merge pass.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to coalesce maintenance windows on the core system, where overlapping or contiguous windows must become the true continuous outage periods so customer communications state accurate downtime. Taking the maximum end handled a window fully contained in another, and using a less-than-or-equal overlap test merged windows that touch end-to-start into one block.

The senior-level point I make is that this sorted-sweep pattern is the backbone of interval scheduling, calendar and booking systems, memory-range coalescing, and genomic range merging, so it is far more than a puzzle. I also connect it to its neighbours: the same idea inserts a new interval into a sorted set, finds free gaps, or counts the maximum number of concurrent intervals, which leads directly into the meeting-rooms problem, so mastering this one unlocks a whole family of interval questions.
